idiom_name: iterator method (yield return) as the unfold + Enumerable.Aggregate as the fold, fused by deferred execution
implementation_notes: An iterator method carrying yield return is the coalgebra: the compiler lowers it to a state machine that produces one element per MoveNext, so the unfold allocates no collection and its local variables are the seed. Composing it with Enumerable.Aggregate (or a foreach loop with an accumulator) performs the fold during the same enumeration, which is the fused recursion - LINQ's deferred execution means the query describes the pipeline instead of materializing it. The two-phase form is still right when the sequence feeds several consumers or repeated enumerations would re-run the producer: materialize once with ToList and fold the data, rather than paying for the generator twice.
pitfalls: An iterator method runs only on the first MoveNext, so argument validation and exceptions surface at consumption time - validate eagerly in a separate wrapper method if that matters.
Enumerating the same IEnumerable twice re-executes the whole unfold (and any side effects); materialize when the producer is expensive.
Enumerable.Aggregate without a seed throws InvalidOperationException on an empty sequence; always pass the identity element for a hylomorphism, whose result must be defined at the terminal case.
